Industry leaders, exhibitors and visitors gather for the fourth edition of the Lantau Yacht Club Boat Show
Hong Kong’s yacht industry is seeking to attract more buyers and visitors from mainland China under a new cross-boundary travel scheme, but relatively high berthing costs could pose a challenge, industry representatives have said.
Industry leaders, exhibitors and visitors gathered in Discovery Bay on Friday for the fourth edition of the Lantau Yacht Club Boat Show, which runs until Sunday.
The show featured more than 30 vessels, including superyachts and models from international brands such as Sunseeker, Princess and Azimut.

articles.title_orig: US job growth surges in October; unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.title_zh: US job growth surges in October; unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.content_orig:
‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December
The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.
Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The unemployment rate went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.
Average hourly earnings increased at an annual rate of 3.1%, slightly higher than last month. Inflation over the last few months has largely outpaced the growth in wages – what often leads people to feel they are spending even more to buy essentials. In September, the annualized inflation rate was 3.7%.
Initial figures for August and September were also revised up by a total of 84,000 jobs. Job growth was seen in healthcare, transportation, warehousing and manufacturing.
Other data released earlier this week showed employment has been steady. Layoffs in September fell to their lowest level in a year and a half, according to the bureau, while outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas tracked just under 44,000 layoffs in October – a 71% decrease compared with last October.
The new data comes after a seismic midterm election that solidified Democrats’ control of Congress for the next two years. Multiple polls had shown Americans were most frustrated about the state of the economy, especially higher gas and grocery prices.
“Americans delivered a clear verdict in the midterm elections that the current economy is squeezing people financially and making it hard to get by, let alone get ahead,” said Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, in a statement before Friday’s report. “The labor market is a good example of why people are frustrated.”
But it’s unclear when Americans will get relief. Gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher than they were a year ago because of the war in Iran. The price of diesel, which is used throughout the supply chain to power large vehicles, is 60% higher compared with prewar levels.
In times of stubborn inflation, the US Federal Reserve usually intervenes by raising interest rates, which slows price increases. In September, the Fed hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023, bringing them up to a range of 3.75%-4%, citing inflation. Though officials kept rates steady at their last meeting in October, held the week before the election, economists are expecting one more rate hikes at the next central bank meeting in December.
Meanwhile, markets over the last week have been shaken as investors appeared worried about AI spending. After reaching correction territory, when an index drops 10% below its most recent peak, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index briefly made a recovery on Wednesday before diving back into correction territory on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: US Stock Rout Pauses as Dip Buyers Offer Support: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: US Stock Rout Pauses as Dip Buyers Offer Support: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
A tech stock rout that began overnight in the United States has persisted in Asian trading.
Market authorities in South Korea paused trading on Friday as prices plunged across the region. Global markets have been rattled by a sharp fall in the trading price of tech stocks, which is driven by fears that the Democrats’ victory in the US midterm elections will increase regulatory scrutiny of AI and slow the country’s data centre build-out.
Japan’s Nikkei index slumped 6 percent, its deepest one-day drop since April 2025. Indices in South Korea and Taiwan plunged more than 8 percent after the opening bell, before cutting losses as authorities scrambled to stem the selling.
Wall Street’s volatility “fear gauge” soared overnight on Thursday and the tech-focused Nasdaq sank 5.5 percent, wiping $3 trillion off S&P 500 firms, as investors fretted that the Democrats could put the brakes on the AI boom being encouraged by President Donald Trump.
“It was a brutal morning for many investors here in Asia. We saw that the AI sell-off continues here across many countries,” Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu reported from Beijing.
“Some of those major markets have fortunately recovered some of those losses, but all of them are still clearly in the red,” she said.
Analysts say the political jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky footing due to worries about returns on massive spending on related infrastructure.
“The selloff shows that AI stock prices had been built on rosy illusions about the future, and now that illusion is gone,” Dong Baozhen, chairman of asset manager Lingtong Shengtai, told the Reuters news agency.
“The US stock market has been the standard-bearer and backbone of the global AI bull run. Now that backbone has snapped. Can AI bull markets elsewhere hold up on their own?”
Markets cut some of their losses by the time Asian markets closed, as authorities worked to stem the panic.
Trading on South Korea’s Kospi market was temporarily halted amid the sharp slide. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il also eased rules on retail investors’ leveraged investments.
In China, state entities stepped in to buy up equities in a bid to stabilise the market, said Al Jazeera’s Yu.
The Taiwan stock market closed down 4.5 percent, recovering somewhat from its early morning slump. For the week, the index clocked a 12.2 percent decline, its biggest since 1991, LSEG data showed.
The government of the island state, a key producer of chips, sought to talk up the prospects for the sector.
Demand ⁠for emerging technologies like AI, ⁠high-performance computing and ⁠cloud services is expected to keep expanding, driving ‌demand for tech companies, the economy ministry said in a statement issued on Friday.
Korean AI chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell nearly 6 percent and 9.4 percent respectively, cutting steep losses from earlier. TSMC fell as much as 8.5 percent in Taiwan, before closing down 4.7 percent.
In Japan, Kioxia plunged 11 percent while AI investor SoftBank Group slid 11 percent.
The selling indicates investors are starting to factor in increased opposition to data centres. Analysts say markets have yet to fully consider the cost such building work has imposed on communities.
Toby Walsh, the chief scientist for the AI Institute at Australia’s University of New South Wales, said he expected new regulations on data centres in many countries, including the US, Australia and the United Kingdom.
“The developers were building them in a way that wasn’t actually getting social licence,” Walsh told Al Jazeera.
“They were building them in places where they didn’t need to build. You don’t have to build data centres in urban areas. You can build them in the middle of nowhere.
“I think it’s actually for the good of the tech industry in the United States that this has happened,” he added. “We’re spending money a bit too quickly. And maybe this is the way to let that bubble deflate in a manageable way.”

articles.title_zh: MP Materials Rare-Earth Earnings Were Rock Solid. What’s Up With the Stock?

Oops, something went wrong
After falling 13.6% in September, MP Materials (NYSE:MP) shares continued to tumble last month. With firms curbing their enthusiasm for the rare-earth stock, investors had sufficient cause to click the sell button.
According to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence , MP Materials stock fell 11.9% in October.

Maintaining an outperform rating, Baird cut its price target 19% to $65 from $80 on Oct. 1. Based on MP Materials stock closing at $47.29 on Sept. 30, Baird's new price target implied upside of 37%.
A few days later, Morgan Stanley adopted a similar perspective on MP Materials stock, slashing its price target to $66 from $73. According to Thefly.com , Morgan Stanley stated in a note on Americas Metals & Mining that it currently prefers precious metal stocks, recognizing "upside to spot gold and silver prices near-term and higher long-term price forecasts."
Later in October, Goldman Sachs also adopted a less optimistic stance, lowering its price target on MP Materials to $57 from $65, while maintaining a buy rating.
MP Materials is an American company that operates throughout the rare-earth supply chain. In addition to owning and operating the Mountain Pass Rare Earth Mine and Processing Facility in California, the company owns and operates Independence, a rare-earth metal, alloy, and magnet manufacturing facility in Texas.
The company has two reportable segments. The materials segment generates revenue primarily from sales of neodymium-praseodymium oxide and metal, mostly sold to customers in the United States, Japan, and South Korea. The magnetics segment includes the Independence facility, which produces and sells magnetic precursor products and rare-earth permanent magnets.
It's not only the last week of October that was challenging for MP Materials. Shares of the rare-earth specialist are currently down about 53% from their 52-week high. While the recent plunge may be alarming, the company hasn't reported anything disastrous that underpins the drop. Instead, it's simply part of a sectorwide decline in rare-earth stocks.

Before doing so, though, investors will want to dig into the company's third-quarter 2026 financial results (expected to be released after the market closes on Nov. 5) to confirm that it's making progress with construction of its 10X facility, a large rare-earth magnet manufacturing facility located in Texas.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq eyes higher open as chips pare losses, rate-hike fears linger
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq eyes higher open as chips pare losses, rate-hike fears linger
articles.content_orig:
Global stock markets have tumbled after investors sold tech shares on fears that the US midterm elections would slow the development of artificial intelligence (AI).
The sell-off, which started in the US and then spread to Asia and Europe, has seen trillions of dollars wiped off the stock value of major tech firms.
In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index sank 5.5% on Thursday. Asian markets also saw hefty falls on Friday and European markets opened lower.
Investors are worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates opposed the data centres needed by the technology. The share falls also come on top of concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
The sell-off in US stocks meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia shares sliding more than 9%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday.
The sharp fall in the Nasdaq meant it lost an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value. The index is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.
However, the huge gains seen by tech stocks in recent times - driven by the enthusiasm for AI - mean that even after Thursday's fall, the Nasdaq is still higher than it was a year ago, and up about 4.6% from where it was at the start of this year.
The US sell-off spread into Asia on Friday. The Nikkei share index in Japan closed down 6% as shares in memory chip makers Kioxia and Tokyo Electron saw big falls.
In South Korea, the Kospi index plunged more than 8% at one point, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling.
The Kospi eventually closed down 6%, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix falling more than 10%.
European markets fell on Friday, although the declines were not as severe as the indexes contain fewer tech stocks. The UK's FTSE 100 index fell nearly 2% while Germany's Dax index was down 2.4%.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said investors were worried about the huge amounts of money being spent on AI with "no clear idea of when, or whether, there will be payback".
"The midterm election result muddied the waters as the Democrats now have more influence and could slow down the pace of data centre roll-outs and look at new ways to regulate the sector," he added.
"The AI story has all been about speed, and now there is a danger of it moving to a lower gear, and some of the wheels falling off."
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in the midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency.
"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday.
Trump blamed the stock slide on his political opponents.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said in a social media post on Thursday.
"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats."
He also appeared to take aim at voters too.
"The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" he wrote on Truth Social.
On Friday, Trump restated his support for the AI sector, saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California.
With additional reporting from Lily Jamali

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Nasdaq futures rebound after brutal sell-off, Dow and S&P 500 wobble as US adds 165K jobs
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Nasdaq futures rebound after brutal sell-off, Dow and S&P 500 wobble as US adds 165K jobs
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks stabilized on Friday after a post-election rally turned into an artificial intelligence trade meltdown, sending tremors through markets. Investors also assessed a hotter-than-expected October jobs report.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.1%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) rose 1%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) gained 1.9% after the tech-heavy index slipped into a correction on Thursday.
The major indexes were on track to post substantial losses during the volatile election week that saw the Democrats retake the House and Senate . At the center of Thursday's deep sell-off, which erased $2.3 trillion in market value, were concerns about a slowdown in data center construction and in AI spending.
The hit chip stocks like Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), AMD ( AMD ), and Sandisk ( SNDK ) most directly, but also spilled into broader markets, sending the VIX Volatility Index ( ^VIX ) up 70% to 28.
Oil prices have also been in play, with global benchmark Brent crude ( BZ=F ) and WTI crude ( CL=F ) futures falling below $100 per barrel. Energy traders continue to assess the outlook for the war in the Middle East, with the potential for a reescalation weighing on sentiment.
Not to be overshadowed, the Labor Department reported that the US added 165,000 jobs in October , above a revised 60,000 figure the month before and the 65,000 jobs economists expected.
Chip stocks rebounded on Friday after suffering their worst sell-off since 2020. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) bounced 4% following a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Shares of US chipmaker Intel ( INTC ) jumped nearly 6%, erasing part of their 10% slide in the prior session. AMD ( AMD ) also rebounded 8% after suffering a 17% fall. Nvidia ( NVDA ), which declined 9% in the prior session, jumped 6%.
Semiconductors bounced back after much of the AI trade was hammered on Thursday as investors digested what a Democratic win in Congress means for the data center build-out in the US.
Memory and storage names Sandisk ( SNDK ), Micron Technology ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) shares tumbled alongside Samsung Electronics ( 005930.KS ) following Thursday's wipeout on Wall Street.
US stocks were mixed at Friday's open as investors looked for more signs that market conditions have stabilized after Thursday's sharp AI-led sell-off.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 0.9%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) rose 0.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) rose more than 1.4%.
Technology shares attempted to rebound after Thursday's rout, which pushed the Nasdaq back into correction territory and erased much of Wednesday's post-election rally.
Investors were also parsing the October jobs report for clues on whether the labor market remains strong enough to keep another Federal Reserve rate hike in play.
Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger reports:
A much stronger-than-expected October jobs report solidifies expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December, as officials are already focused on higher inflation.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics report released Friday showed that 165,000 jobs were created in October , compared with expectations for around 70,000, as the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, compared with expectations for 4.2%. That's much higher than the average monthly gain of 48,000 over the past 12 months and well above the roughly 30,000 jobs needed to hold employment steady. Labor force participation inched up to a hair above expectations at 61.9%.
Job gains in both August and September were also revised higher by 84,000. The bulk of jobs added were in the sectors of professional and business services, healthcare, and transportation and warehousing. Manufacturing added 19,000 jobs.
The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, a jump from the revised job growth of 60,000 the month before. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expected the economy to have added 65,000 jobs.
The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%. Wage growth increased 0.4% from September.
If you are looking for something positive after Thursday's shocking stock beatdown , you have come to the right place ahead of the weekend.
History suggests stocks tend to do well after the extreme volatility we saw two days removed from the Election Day blue wave.
The VIX volatility index ( ^VVIX ) — better known as Wall Street's fear gauge — jumped as much as 70% on Thursday. A move this large has only happened eight times since 1991, according to data from CBOE.
Here's what happened to the S&P 500 on average after the eight prior extreme moves:
1 month later: +3.0% (7 of 8 times positive)
3 months later: +7.1% (6 of 8 times positive)
6 months later: +10.4% (8 of 8 times positive)
1 year later: +14.7% (7 of 8 times positive)
The stock market's Thursday rout in artificial intelligence boom trade may have been an overreaction to growing political opposition to data center construction, according to one prominent bull.
AI and chip stocks plunged Thursday as major indexes erased their post-midterm election rally. One key worry is that about 45% of planned US data center capacity faces possible restrictions after tallying newly elected state governors who have promised to stop or pause construction, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.
But Yardeni Research is calling those mounting restrictions a setback.
"We view the political backlash as another constraint on AI investment, alongside financial and physical bottlenecks. But these are speed bumps, not roadblocks, even though Wall Street seems to be pricing in the latter," Yardeni Research wrote in a Friday note to clients.
"We think that's overdone," the strategists said, referring to Thursday's sell-off as a "buying opportunity." The firm is sticking with its year-end target of 7,900 on the S&P 500.
Yardeni pointed to Texas, a major data center hub, where newly elected governor Gina Hinojosa said Thursday afternoon in a CNN interview that already permitted projects would be allowed to finish construction.
The distinction matters. Permitted data center projects account for "essentially all of Texas's planned data center capacity in 2027 and likely much of 2028," according to Yardeni.
Employment data scheduled for release on Friday is expected to show the labor market remains steady. Yahoo Finance's Claire Boston previews what to expect from today's jobs report:
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect that the economy added 65,000 jobs in October, an improvement from September's underwhelming 29,000 additions. The unemployment rate is expected to hold steady at 4.2%, while wage growth is seen improving 0.3% from September.
Those numbers would be consistent with the "low hire, low fire" environment that has defined the labor market for the past several years. While few companies are hiring aggressively, most aren't conducting major layoffs either.
Recent initial jobless claims have looked "exceptionally benign by historical standards," Bank of America economist Shruti Mishra wrote in a note.
"Despite recent high-profile layoff announcements, the absence of any pickup in claims suggests economy-wide layoffs remain contained," she added.
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
When President Trump and his allies in Congress moved to end the EV subsidy, automakers braced for a crash in electric car sales. Tesla ( TSLA ), the US leader, was especially vulnerable because it didn't have gas-powered vehicles to lean on, and keeping prices as low as possible was crucial to competing with EV rivals.
But those initial worries gave way to optimism.
In a new regulatory environment, one that was more hostile to EVs, Tesla used the disappearing $7,500 tax break as an advantage . It lost a valuable subsidy, but used its scale to win a war of attrition, thereby consolidating the market. Other firms needed the subsidy even more, and though Tesla got hurt, the damage was less than its peers' in many ways.

articles.title_orig: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.title_zh: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.content_orig:
Just over three weeks ago, the most significant visit of Pope Leo’s pontificate looked to be in doubt. The 71-year-old’s lung cancer surgery led some in the Vatican to believe his trip to Latin America would be postponed or its intense schedule adjusted.
But Leo XIV is forging ahead with a grueling 12-day visit, which includes Uruguay, Argentina, and an emotional “homecoming” to Peru, the country where he served as a missionary and bishop for around two decades.
He plans to cover a lot of ground – around 19,000 miles – while in Latin America. From November 6 to 17, the pope is scheduled to take 14 flights (including two in a helicopter), give 36 speeches and participate in around 50 events in what is one of the most intense papal trips of recent years.
He will also visit Cusco, Peru, which is more than 11,000 feet above sea-level and where there is 35% less oxygen per breath. During the whole trip, he’ll travel to 10 cities, preside at large open-air Masses and vigils and meet with political leaders.
The trip, especially Cusco’s altitude, has raised questions about his health and the precautions being taken while there. It has also shone a light on a region that has profoundly shaped him and set his path to the papacy.
The pontiff had surgery last month to remove a third of his right lung after a small growth was discovered during routine checks, which was later confirmed as cancer. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said afterward that there were “no clinical reasons why this visit should not take place,” and doctors have said he does not need further treatment.
Vatican officials told reporters that Pope Leo will have a medical team available to him for the trip but stressed that no special measures are being taken. “We’re speaking of a 71-year-old person in good health,” the Vatican spokesman said ahead of the visit.
He explained the pope will travel with the “ordinary medical assistance,” including doctors, nurses and an ambulance, which usually travels with the pope’s convoy. But the spokesman said he wasn’t going into too much detail as the pope does not have a “permanent condition.” And if the Vatican medical team needs any help, one of the journalists traveling with the pope is also a doctor.
Montse Alvarado, the new head of Vatican Communications, told journalists on Tuesday that the pope’s “stamina is fantastic,” and that “he’ll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen.”
Dr. Matthew Triplette, a pulmonologist from the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle, told CNN the risk of a medical emergency during the trip is “low” but that this could include “either a collapsed lung or blood clots.”
Triplette said the pope may be advised to “take low-dose blood thinners or use exercises or compression devices” to lower the possibility of blood clots in his legs when flying, which could cause major issues if they spread to the lungs. He added that the pope may feel more fatigue with exertion, particularly because there is less oxygen available at altitude.
In the aftermath of his surgery, many speculated that the trip would be canceled.
“I must confess that, until just a few days ago, I was among the few who had serious doubts about whether this trip could even take place,” Guzmán Carriquiry, a Uruguayan former Vatican official who worked on Latin American issues for nearly 50 years in the church’s central administration, told reporters on Tuesday.
But he also pointed out that the pope’s health team gave him the green light. “This suggests that his doctors believe the pope possesses a robust physical constitution; it also serves as a testament to the pope’s ardent desire and determination to go out and meet our people,” he said.
But Carriquiry noted that he would have removed Cusco from the agenda if he had organized the trip.
While Leo XIV is known for his gentle, low-key style, he is determined.
Answering a question from CNN, Alvarado said the pope “personally confirmed this trip with no changes,” and that he was looking forward to returning to Latin America.
The continent, and Peru in particular, is close to his heart, and Alvarado said the pope would speak off the cuff frequently in Spanish, a language he is fluent in.
“He’s going on this trip very simply because he wants to go,” is how Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican foreign minister, put it at an event in Rome at the end of last month.
The Peruvian part of the trip will be emotional, as Leo arrives there “as an adopted brother, adopted by the Peruvian people,” said Carriquiry.
The pope, who remains a Peruvian citizen, had three stints in Peru, having first arrived there in his 30s. He also served as Bishop of Chiclayo in the northwest part of the country from 2015 to 2023.
The pope will return to Chiclayo during the trip and is expected to receive a rapturous welcome. Leo is remembered fondly in the city, where he was considered a hands-on bishop who was known to travel across his diocese on horseback.
“The pope spent many years living amongst the simple, poor and devout people of rural Latin America in northern Peru, as a missionary and a pastor,” Carriquiry, who is the former secretary of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, said.
Leo is expected to draw huge crowds when he’s there, with estimates of around 1.2 million people expected to attend his final Mass of the trip at Las Palmas Airbase in Lima.
He is also expected to draw huge crowds in Argentina, where more than a million people are expected to attend his Mass in Buenos Aires.
The late Pope Francis, the first Argentine pontiff, never made a visit to his home country, so Leo’s visit is one that is generating intense interest.
Francis never gave a clear reason as to why he didn’t visit Argentina. Carriquiry, a close friend of the late pope, said it “remains an enigma.”
Leo XIV’s visit will underline his plans to continue the reforms of his predecessor, but with his own distinctive style.
The pope’s visit comes at a time when Argentine President Javier Milei’s “chainsaw” austerity measures have led to welfare spending cuts. Milei has also equated state-led social justice programs with communism.
Pope Leo, in contrast, has made the church’s social teaching and concern for the marginalized a central concern of his papacy. His itinerary includes a visit to a federal prison in Buenos Aires and a stop at a care center for people with intellectual and physical disabilities in Claypole which has been affected by the Milei cuts.
Both Milei and Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori are notable figures in Latin America’s right-wing surge. They also enjoy support from the Trump administration, which Leo has publicly disagreed with — particularly on migration issues.
Leo XIV would not have been elected pope had he not been sent to Peru as a young Augustinian missionary.
His time in Latin America put him on a path to be spotted by Pope Francis. It was Francis who appointed the then-Rev. Robert Prevost as bishop in Chiclayo before later bringing him to Rome and naming him a cardinal.
All of this set him up as a candidate in the 2025 conclave. While Leo is the first pope from the United States and grew up in Chicago, his experience in Latin America has profoundly influenced his outlook.
In Peru, he served in the birthplace of liberation theology, a movement focused on social and political action to help the poor and oppressed. As a bishop, he was known for organizing practical assistance for those affected by floods or in need of medical equipment during the Covid-19 pandemic.
He served in a church in Peru which emphasized an inclusive model, giving greater roles to those not ordained as priests and bishops, including women.
Leo’s time in Peru also saw him exposed to the fallout of the clerical abuse crisis, including a major scandal involving a powerful Catholic group . The Vatican says the pope will have two meetings with abuse survivors during his trip, one in Argentina and another in Peru.

articles.title_orig: Newsroom bomb threats follow escalating European flight hoaxes
articles.title_zh: Newsroom bomb threats follow escalating European flight hoaxes
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of flights and several media organizations across Europe this week have been impacted by a string of hoax bomb threats which have disrupted travel plans and left authorities scrambling to identify the culprit.
Fresh disruption hit several European airports and flights on Friday while Ireland’s national broadcaster RTÉ evacuated its offices after also receiving a bomb threat. Several other media organizations, including Sky, said they too had received similar threats.
This string of incidents comes as Europe grapples with more and more hybrid attacks, some of which authorities have blamed on Russia though it remains unclear exactly who is directing this latest wave of threats.
Here’s what we know so far.
Initially, these threats targeted airports and airlines. On Friday, police in Denmark and the Czech Republic said that fresh threats had been directed toward air traffic at Copenhagen and Prague airports, respectively, while Hungary’s defense minister said fighter jets escorted three planes in the country’s airspace reporting a threat on Friday morning.
A KLM flight traveling from Prague to Amsterdam was searched when it landed too but no explosives were found on board, Dutch authorities told national broadcaster NOS. And that all came after at least 14 flights were impacted by similar threats on Thursday.
Threats targeting media organizations, mostly in Ireland, emerged later on Friday too. An RTÉ reporter read excerpts of the email received by the outlet in which someone claimed to be planning to blow up Europe’s “airplanes, cruise ships, subway stations and trains.”
“We want the whole world to know about us which is why one of our operatives has planted an explosive device in your building,” the email said, according to PA Media. “It will detonate in 45 minutes, the clock is ticking.”
It’s not completely clear, although Czech and Italian authorities say they were made by email.
A representative of Václav Havel Airport in Prague, told CNN the threats it received about bombs being placed on four flights were made in an anonymous email.
A Czech Police spokesperson told CNN the email was addressed to the airport, adding that similar emails were sent to other airports in Europe.
The Italy flight threats came in an email from an anti-feminist group calling itself “The Male State” to a logistics hub company working with Rome Fiumicino Airport.
The email, first published by CNN Affiliate SkyTG24, made the false claim that “explosive devices” had been placed on two flights - one from Helsinki and another from Dublin. A spokesperson for the airport confirmed to CNN the screenshot was authentic.
The International Centre for Counter-Terrorism, a Netherlands-based think tank, said “The Male State,” was created in Russia in 2016 as a misogynist movement, that later emerged as a vocal supporter of the Ukraine war. A Russian court banned the group and labelled it as an extremist organization in 2021.
All European airports plan and carry out training for incidents like these. Speaking to CNN, Keith Jeffries, a former Federal Security Director at LAX airport, said that all airports “will have bomb threat management plans, and they’ll train to that plan,” allowing them to make decisions in a matter of seconds.
The bottom line is that no aviation authority will ever ignore a bomb threat, Jeffries said.
Again, it remains unclear at this stage who exactly was behind the threats. No official group or state has been identified by any European country at this stage. The European Union has said it is too early to say whether the incidents are linked.
Security analysts and government ministers have suggested it could be part of a wider hybrid campaign or series of malicious hoaxes.
Eric Schouten, the head of aviation security group Dyami, suggested saboteurs acting on behalf of the Russian state could be to blame.
“From railways to the food infrastructure that you see happening with the fridges being hacked ⁠and all ​kinds of other operations, it does fit the narrative of Russian state actors ​who want to disturb Europe,” Schouten said, according to Reuters. He also pointed out that many of the countries affected have supported Ukraine in its war with Russia.
Germany’s foreign ministry made reference to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine too, saying that Europe’s security is “being tested far beyond the Ukrainian frontline.” The ministry referenced these bomb threats, the cyberattacks on supermarket fridges and drones crossing into some European countries’ airspace as examples of such threats.
Similarly, Spain’s foreign minister José Manuel Albares said “the most reasonable assumption is that we are facing an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare.”
The UK’s transport minister Heidi Alexander, meanwhile, described the threats as a “malicious hoax.”
Authorities steered clear of naming any specific culprit, however. Irish official Simon Harris told Cork 96FM “we don’t yet know whether it’s an individual behind this effort” to target the country’s media outlets, “or some part of a coordinated effort.”
Overall, the impact has been relatively contained. All the threats have so far proven false, with the authorities involved saying that no such explosive devices have been found.
They have, of course, caused disruption to travelers. The passengers and crew on at least 14 planes were impacted on Thursday, including an Aer Lingus flight bound for Rome that was diverted to France and two flights from Spain and Denmark that were forced to divert to Bulgarian capital Sofia. It comes after at least seven flights were rerouted on Tuesday.
Analysts are warning the threats could be aimed at both causing disruption and observing the response from airlines and authorities.
“These aviation threats are also occurring in the same period as cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe,” Eliran Almog, CEO of aviation cybersecurity firm Cyviation, told Reuters.
“Different essential services are experiencing disruption that carries economic costs and can undermine public confidence.”
CNN’s Seb Shukla, Pau Mosquera, Ivana Kottasová, Stefano Pozzebon, Charlotte Reck, Sana Noor Haq and Magdalena Sofia Vitores Moreno contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Peru airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
articles.title_zh: Peru airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
articles.content_orig:
Three suitcases’ worth of the spiders were on their way to Germany, where they could fetch an estimated €1.5m
More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.
The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.
They were spotted after agents noticed some unusual wriggling inside the luggage during a routine customs inspection at Jorge Chávez international airport. “We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones,” said Cora Suarez, a SERFOR wildlife control technician.
One tarantula can sell for about €500 ($560) in Europe, Suarez said, meaning the wildlife trafficking scheme would be potentially worth €1.5m for just one trip.
The hidden arachnids, which came from several regions of Peru, were found in varying stages of development, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, Suarez said.
The Europeans accused of smuggling the tarantulas were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and will face criminal proceedings, SERFOR said.
Illegal wildlife trafficking is a highly lucrative criminal activity that generates around $20bn annually worldwide, according to Interpol.
Such trafficking is among the primary causes of the loss of biodiversity on the planet.

articles.title_orig: Activists breach Microsoft data centre construction site as protests spread in Europe
articles.title_zh: Activists breach Microsoft data centre construction site as protests spread in Europe
articles.content_orig:
Europe is witnessing a wave of protests against data centers.
Europe is witnessing a wave of protests against data centers.
Protesters have broken into a construction site of a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam this morning. Members of the Geef Tegengas group helped organize the protest against the construction of three 85-meter data center towers in the outskirts of Amsterdam.
Reuters reports that around 100 people made it into the construction site, with some scaling a crane to place a “fuck AI” banner. Protesters also unfurled a “Microsoft powers genocide” banner on the construction site, and chanted “Microsoft has got to go” and “free Palestine.”
Opposition to the new data center in Amsterdam comes more than a year after the city banned new data centers until 2030, after a temporary stop that was announced at the end of 2023. Microsoft will be the sole tenant of this new data center, and the project is proceeding as it was planned as far back as 2016, before a ban was put in place. The site, being built by British developer Pure Data Centres, has also managed to navigate some loopholes to reach the construction stage.
The protests over Microsoft’s data center site in Amsterdam comes in the same week that activists staged a mock Israeli military checkpoint outside a Microsoft data center in Dublin on Tuesday, part of a wave of data center protests across Europe . Earlier this week, voters across the US also rejected unrestrained development of data centers. AI data centers are continuing to pop up across the US, with frequent opposition from locals concerned about the impact on their communities.
Microsoft also abandoned the UK’s largest data center project last month, after local electricity grid officials said the site won’t be supplied with power until the 2030s. The software maker has also faced a wave of protests from former employees over the past year. Microsoft’s 50th anniversary party was interrupted by employees protesting the use of Microsoft’s technologies in Israel’s war against Hamas, with one calling Microsoft’s AI CEO, Mustafa Suleyman, a “war profiteer .“
A Microsoft employee also disrupted the company’s Build developer conference last year, interrupting Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella’s keynote. Months later, Microsoft fired two employee protesters who occupied its president’s office.

articles.title_orig: After a $2.5 Trillion Wipeout, Tech Investors Brace for More Pain
articles.title_zh: After a $2.5 Trillion Wipeout, Tech Investors Brace for More Pain
articles.content_orig:

E very silver lining has a cloud, if you’ll pardon the pun. And so the unexpected Democrat “blue tsunami” that swept the US midterms has apparently exacerbated the big tech sell-off that has been quietly rumbling for some time, albeit until now not attracting many headlines outside the financial pages .
Trillions of dollars have been wiped off the stock value of major tech firms overnight in the US, Europe and Asia amid concerns of a slowdown in AI development.
There are fears that a Democrat-controlled Congress and newly installed blue governors in states such as Texas will pass laws, impose regulations and generally stymie the previously uninhibited growth in returns from already bloated AI investment.
If lawmakers won’t let the likes of OpenAI, X and Anthropic regulate themselves, and if state legislators won’t permit data centres to be built where residents don’t want them, then the industry will grow more slowly and generate lower profits. Therefore there’s less point in putting investors’ cash into them.
Hence what is now a general “correction” – a broad loss of about 10 per cent of value – rather than a crash. There’s still enough faith in the future of AI for it to attract investors who don’t want to be left with outdated portfolios – a useful “Fomo” effect. But there is also sufficient nerves, ignorance and lack of transparency around these new tech giants, AI itself, chipmakers and hardware firms, that valuations and share prices will be volatile.
We’ve seen such gyrations before, notably in the internet dot-com boom and crash around 2000, but also in previous over-excited booms such as railway mania of the 19th century. The good news is that although some investors are ruined, such over-exuberance leaves behind a socially useful legacy and some sound companies. This time, the scale of the money involved is unprecedented, so, as with the mooted flotation of Anthropic, a scaling back from $2 trillion to $1.5 trillion has an oversized impact. The same goes for ChatGPT , which has reduced a routine round of private fundraising from $30bn to $20bn. Another factor is the way highly leveraged hedge funds have piled in, drawing on private equity – and have all been placing their bets in the same direction.
They’ve also been running into trouble. There is also a significant Chinese sector, which, ironically, has many more publicly quoted AI companies than the US, based on an open access model. In New York, the only real examples are Alphabet, which owns Google and much else, plus Elon Musk’s SpaceX . Some disappointing numbers from Google the other day triggered a substantial fall in the share price, an early harbinger of the current turmoil. In any case, the average punter can get immediate exposure to the AI boom much more easily in China, which has its downsides when things get rocky. Out in Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Tech index, comprising 30 major technology companies, is down 30 per cent year to date.
Boom and bust then, which is normal for capitalism. But central banks and governments, at least in most of the West, will now find it extremely difficult to insulate their wider economies from a crash. This is something that Andrew Bailey , governor of the Bank of England, has been warning about, rightly, for some time. The problem now is that the levels of public debt and interest rates make it harder for the authorities to intervene to prevent a sectoral collapse from transmuting into a global recession. We were able to launch a massive international rescue campaign when the banks failed during the global financial crisis in 2008 and after.
The crash of 1987 was swiftly ameliorated by the Fed – the “Greenspan Put”, which has reassured market players in succeeding decades. Much the same goes for the aftershocks in the eurozone crises around 2011, bailed out by German public money, and we even managed to stop Covid from turning into a Great Recession by mortgaging our economies, borrowing a year’s worth of GDP. This time around, because we have less room for manoeuvre, it’s harder to see how the wider world economy can be cushioned from a tech sell-off that could easily turn into a panic, wiping billions off the value of people’s pensions, among other terrible consequences, as Donald Trump has rather gleefully pointed out. China and America won’t cooperate for geopolitical reasons, and Europe is irrelevant. So we find ourselves in the strange position that AI will ruin us before it makes us all rich, and we mere humans can’t understand why.

articles.title_orig: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
articles.title_zh: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
articles.content_orig:
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result
The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party .
The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.
The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.
The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.
In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts , uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.
With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.
Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.
after newsletter promotion
The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.
With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs .
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

articles.title_orig: Data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.title_zh: Data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.content_orig:
Alpha Compute CEO Brittany Kaiser argues that common-sense regulations, not sweeping bans or moratoriums, are the key to unlocking economic growth while protecting local communities.
President Donald Trump has thrown the federal government's weight behind massive data center build-outs needed to power the country's artificial intelligence (AI) boom. But a historic Democratic sweep in Texas has put one of the nation's biggest AI infrastructure hubs under new political leadership, raising questions about the future of billions of dollars in planned investments.
The victories marked a historic midterm night for Texas Democrats, who captured the governor's mansion for the first time in more than three decades and won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1988.
Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. data center power capacity through 2030. With at least 248 projects planned across the state, investment bank Jefferies estimates that 13.3 gigawatts of announced developments could be at risk under a moratorium backed by Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa.
ONE STATE IS GROUND ZERO AS TRUMP'S MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR TECH AMBITIONS FACE A MIDTERM TEST
Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. capacity through 2030. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Texas was hardly alone in facing growing opposition to data center development. In Ohio, voters weighed 21 data center-related ballot questions across 18 communities in the midterm elections, more than any other state , highlighting the mounting resistance to America's rapidly expanding AI infrastructure.
The results this week are now forcing some developers to reconsider where to invest billions of dollars in future projects as political power shifts.
"It makes us and our investors pause and think if we should be investing somewhere else," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital following the Republican bloodbath in Tuesday's election.
Kaiser warned that political shifts in traditionally Republican states could push billions of dollars in planned investments elsewhere, including overseas, as companies weigh growing opposition to data center development — especially within the Democratic Party.
"There's new decision making that needs to come into play and a lot more to think about than there was before the election," she said.
IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE’S WHAT WE SAW
A data center stores and processes the digital information that powers services people use every day. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
But relocating projects already underway is far more complicated, particularly when developers have secured land, negotiated power agreements and committed substantial capital.
"It's not very easy to pivot after you've already made contractual and financial commitments to these types of builds," Kaiser said.
For projects still in the pipeline, however, companies have more flexibility. Kaiser said Alpha Compute has already invested in data centers in Canada, Europe and Mexico, where regulatory approvals are more straightforward.
The backlash highlights growing tensions between Washington's push to accelerate AI development and voters' concerns about electricity costs and the impact of data centers on their communities.
Kaiser urged incoming lawmakers to strike a balance between addressing community concerns and preserving what she called "the biggest economic opportunity of our generation."
The AI boom is accelerating demand for data centers across Texas as companies seek more space, power and infrastructure to support increasingly intensive computing needs. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It's really important, yes, to make sure that data center companies are good actors and are doing things the right way," she said, calling for "common sense legislation and regulation" that allows developers to work with lawmakers and local communities.
"If we can abide by those rules, then bans and moratoriums should not be the answer," Kaiser said. "It's just let's sensibly regulate and move forward in a way that is positively impactful for communities."
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

articles.title_orig: IRS adjusts 2027 tax brackets. How your paycheck changes
articles.title_zh: IRS adjusts 2027 tax brackets. How your paycheck changes
articles.content_orig:
The IRS announced Thursday adjustments to tax year 2027, including increases to the standard deduction. NBC6’s Valerie Ryan reports
The Internal Revenue Service announced higher federal tax brackets for the 2027 tax year, along with increases to the standard deduction and child tax credit.
The changes will be reflected in tax returns filed in 2028.
Watch NBC6 free wherever you are
The IRS adjusts tax brackets every year for inflation. This way, a household that reports nominally higher income — but not an increase in buying power — doesn’t tip over into a higher bracket.
The new federal income tax brackets come as Americans continue to wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing, groceries, gas and other expenses.
There are also adjustments to the long-term capital gains brackets, estate tax exemption and more. Here's a breakdown of all the changes.
Taxable income determines what rate you pay. This includes income from employment and other sources, minus retirement account contributions, healthcare account contributions, student loan interest and other deductions.
The IRS has also increased the standard deduction, or the amount a household can write off if they choose not to itemize their deductions.
Standard deductions for the 2027 tax year will be $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, an increase of $1,000 from 2026. Single filers can claim $16,600, an increase of $500 from this year, and for heads of households, the standard deduction will be $24,925.
The child tax credit will also increase by $100. For 2027, the maximum credit will be $2,300 per qualifying child under the age of 17 with a valid Social Security number. The maximum refundable portion of the credit will be $1,800, also an increase of $100 from the previous year.
The Earned Income Tax Credit is increasing to a maximum of $8,496 for qualifying taxpayers who have three or more children, up from $8,231in 2026.
The IRS has also given the lifetime gift and estate tax exemption a boost. Wealthy Americans will be able to give their heirs up to $15.48 million in 2027 tax-free. The exemption applies to tax-free transfers during life and at death.
The IRS also increased the exclusion amount for annual gifts. The first $20,000 of gifts to any person are not included in the total amount of taxable gifts made during the year – up from $19,000 in 2026. Meanwhile, personal exemptions will remain at zero, as they did in 2026.
The maximum allowable credit for adoption expenses will rise to $18,250, of which up to $5,280 may be refundable.
The IRS also made changes to benefits: the health flexible spending account contributions will increase to $3,500 and the amount of unused funds that can be carried over will be $700.

Shares of memory chipmaker Micron Technology ( MU ) tumbled 17% as a chip sell-off deepened on Thursday.
Peer SK Hynix ( SKHY ), along with memory and storage names Sandisk ( SNDK ), Seagate ( STX ), and Western Digital ( WDC ), were all down double-digit percentages.
Shares of Micron and other chip stocks declined significantly over the past month amid growing worries of an overextension of the AI trade. The sell-off gained steam on Thursday after Democrats won control of both the House and Senate, raising concerns about a slowdown in data center buildouts.
AI chipmakers Nvidia ( NVDA ) and AMD ( AMD ) sank 9% and 17%, respectively, on Thursday. Broadcom ( AVGO ) also sank 10%.
The carnage among chipmakers was across the board, as seen on Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace chart.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank 12%, leading the Nasdaq Composite into correction territory.

articles.title_orig: How the College Board Is Fighting A.I. Cheating on the SAT Tests
articles.title_zh: How the College Board Is Fighting A.I. Cheating on the SAT Tests
articles.content_orig:
Students walk through Duke University.
“What are some ways a 16-year-old girl is similar to Nick Carraway?”
That was the first question I ever asked AI. I was a sophomore in high school, stuck on a homework assignment about The Great Gatsby —until my Dad called me over to his computer, itching to show me a new technology called ChatGPT.
I gave it the prompt for my essay. In seconds, the screen was filled with flawlessly written ways to compare myself to Gatsby ’s narrator. But something didn’t feel right about taking the chatbot’s answer and pretending it was my own. I challenged myself to ignore its suggestions and come up with my own ideas.
Within weeks, my high school was buzzing about AI. Some of my fellow students in Mr. Brown’s AP Lit class used it to summarize Robert Frost poems, without bothering to read them. I remained torn. An extra hour to chill at home would’ve been nice, but Frost’s poetry wasn’t especially dense. Plus, Mr. Brown was my favorite teacher, and I felt he was owed the effort of doing the reading myself. We all got similar grades on the assignment, which annoyed me. But in our seminar conversation, I could tell I had a deeper understanding of Frost’s work.
In 2024, I got into my dream school, Duke. I couldn’t wait. I longed for the classic collegiate experience my parents described: staying up late discussing philosophy in dorm rooms, reading classic literature in mortared lecture halls, asking life’s biggest questions in the birthplace of scientific discoveries.
I quickly learned that at a school like Duke, efficiency matters as much as accomplishment. The faster you complete your coursework, the more time you can put into the extracurricular activities designed to give you an advantage when you enter the work world. Before classes even began, students were running around campus in suits, rushing pre-professional clubs with lower acceptance rates than Duke itself. Talk of summer internships sprouted around the 8-week mark. The question on everyone’s lips was how to get an A while spending as little time on their schoolwork as possible.
That question isn’t new. It’s always been possible to cut corners or even cheat. But it used to take some level of effort, craft, and intentional deceit. AI makes it frictionless, adding a game-changing weapon to the achievement arms race, the effects of which reverberate beyond the classroom. Students who offload their coursework to AI can devote themselves to the clubs, internships, and leadership roles that become the standard everyone is measured against when interviewing for jobs. AI tilts the playing field against students who care about using their four precious college years for self-discovery and intellectual exploration.
As my homework piled up, I noticed others around me using AI. These were brilliant kids. They had to know something I didn’t. So I made a rule: I would use AI for busywork, but never the subjects I loved. Classmates I admired taught me the art of effective prompts, and I halved my homework time. A boring worksheet that would take my human brain two hours to complete took my augmented intellect only 45 minutes. The arrangement felt perfect: I cut out mindless tasks to preserve my mind for more important assignments.
But as the year progressed, it didn’t take long for my rule to crumble. First, I used AI to summarize a dense reading for my philosophy class, a subject I loved, so I could devote more time to writing a contemplative essay. Then, intoxicated by my new efficiency, I asked AI to help me craft an outline for the essay, so I could concentrate on honing my word choice. It nailed the nuances I struggled to capture. I filled in the chatbot’s outline like a paint-by-numbers and submitted the results. I felt proud of the A I received, as if I had unlocked the future of productivity. For my next assignment, I went to the machine first.
Judgment day came when I got assigned a paper on political polarization. This was my favorite topic of the semester, and I was eager to leave class so I could start drafting. I wanted to savor the process of writing this piece, so I decided to do it the old-fashioned way: just a blank document and my brain. To my surprise, no words flowed onto the page. After a few minutes of total brain freeze, I remembered that I used to start my drafts by jotting down some relevant opinions, stats, and anecdotes. That came easily—but staring at the jumbled fragments, I realized to my horror that I had no idea how to transform them into a coherent piece of writing.
After some intense frustration and effort, my sense of writing eventually came back to me,  but my unsettlement lingered. I struggled to justify the hours spent on that essay rather than on my extracurriculars. I also couldn’t believe how much of myself I had lost to AI.
It scared me. Like a drug, my relationship with AI had become all-or-nothing. I had to cut it out completely.
Immediately, I experienced withdrawal. At times I would get so frustrated at being stuck that I’d open Claude in a browser and then shut down my computer to stop myself. I realized just how little patience I had left for the kind of intellectual challenges I’d been so eager to experience at Duke. What makes AI insidious is that we realize what we’ve lost only in hindsight, when we can no longer summon the perseverance needed for the tasks we used to find pleasurable.
It’s now been nearly four years since the release of generative AI, and I’m well into my sophomore year of college. My schedule is thick with extracurriculars and leadership roles, none of which I’m willing to give up. I resolved not to use AI this semester to substitute for doing my own thinking—even in my philosophy course, where our professor requires us to submit 1,000-word reflections on 150 pages of dense philosophical readings every week. Let me be clear: I would never judge a fellow student for using AI. In my eyes, it is a luxury to be able to spend time being curious.
I see a crossroads ahead. What kind of life do I want to live? One where I’m willing to sacrifice professional advancement for the sake of intellectual curiosity and passion? Or one where I get praised, get ahead, and remain on the cusp of humanity’s technological progress?
It’s tempting to believe that the machine extends my mind, that it’s possible to balance my own intellect with that of the chatbot. But I’ve seen how quickly and quietly AI can rob me of something at my very core. I stand torn between the lures of inner virtue and societal praise. Like Nick Carraway, I am “within and without,” drawn to a glittering new world, yet repulsed by its emotional emptiness. Nick eventually leaves Gatsby’s mansion and returns home to seek a quieter, more fulfilling life.
It remains to be seen how much we have in common.

articles.title_orig: Former pro-democracy lawmaker sentenced to 12½ years in Macao’s first national security case
articles.title_zh: Former pro-democracy lawmaker sentenced to 12½ years in Macao’s first national security case
articles.content_orig:
FILE -Veteran pro-democracy former lawmaker Au Kam San poses for a photo during an interview in Macao, Oct. 7, 2024. Bertha Wang/AP hide caption
HONG KONG — Macao pro-democracy former lawmaker Au Kam San was sentenced to 12½ years in prison Friday in the Chinese casino hub's first national security case following a closed-door trial that raised concerns about fairness.
Au's arrest last year was the first publicly known prosecution under Macao's national security law since it was enacted in 2009. A Macao court found him guilty of subverting state power, breaching confidentiality and establishing contact with organizations, groups or people outside Macao to commit acts endangering national security.
Critics said that his case reflected Beijing's emphasis on security and intolerance of dissent, even though Macao's pro-democracy movement has never been as influential as that in neighboring Hong Kong.
The 69-year-old assisted and cooperated with "hostile organizations" outside Macao for a long period of time in collecting and disseminating political views laden with ideas of subverting state power and false information, according to a court statement. They conspired to incite hatred among Macao residents against the central government, with an intent to overthrow and undermine the country's fundamental system, it said.
"Although the defendant is a first-time offender and admitted to a considerable portion of the criminal facts, he demonstrated a high degree of intent. The degree of unlawfulness and the potential consequences of his crimes are both very serious," the statement said.
Macao is a former Portuguese colony that has operated, like Hong Kong, as a special administrative region since its return to Chinese rule in 1999.
In a public letter, Au's wife, Virginia Cheang, wrote that she only hoped authorities would allow his family to exchange letters with Au and visit him regularly without conditions.
"From a closed-door trial to a public verdict, what kind of operation is this? It's a political trial and it's a groundless persecution to humiliate one's character," Cheang said.
Au's daughter in London, Au Hon I, told The Associated Press that her father is a peaceful family man who cares deeply about Macao, and the thought of him spending more time in prison without having done anything criminal was unbearable. She said that a lawyer earlier arranged by her family wasn't able to see him.
She felt that the ruling was setting boundaries of what citizens can do and what rights they have, saying "it's a very scary chapter that they're starting."
"It just doesn't feel like a safe space anymore being in Macao. And it's very heartbreaking," she said.
The court said that a lawyer approved by Au was appointed to act for him during the legal proceedings, and that he had exercised his right to a defense. The court also approved his family's request to visit him regularly.
Jorge Menezes, a Portuguese lawyer who practices in Macao, said that the trial was held in secret and that specific details — which organizations were involved and what information Au had provided to them — weren't revealed. Menezes noted that the statement said that Au had acknowledged some facts and it might have led people to believe that he had confessed to the crimes.
"From what I see, he did not plead guilty. Otherwise, they would have said. So this is misleading and unfortunate," he said. "It violates his dignity."
He said that Au's case was used to send a message to Macao residents that it was about anyone who challenges the authorities. The case could also carry a message for Hong Kong, because Macao is "a sort of laboratory" for the financial hub in situations like this.
Michael Polak, Au's international counsel, urged Portugal and the European Union to demand that Au, a Portuguese citizen, be allowed to leave Macao.
"A sentence like that for someone of that age is a sentence for life," he said. "If he was left in Macao, he could die in prison."
Macao has its own political and legal systems and Macao is the only Chinese city where casino gambling is legal. It has resorts run by affiliates of the American gaming companies MGM Resorts, Las Vegas Sands and Wynn Resorts.
The court found that Au helped overseas organizations spread false and distorted information between 2023 and 2024 to induce foreign countries to take hostile actions against China and Macao, incite hatred against the central government and undermine the smooth running of the 2024 city leader election.
As a lawmaker in 2021, Au leaked to overseas groups confidential information obtained during closed-door committee meetings over the renewal of gaming licenses, it said.
Au's trial was held behind closed doors in September.
The court earlier said that the judge decided against an open trial to ensure that national security interests wouldn't be undermined.
Au, a teacher-turned-lawmaker, served in the legislature dominated by Beijing loyalists for 20 years before stepping down in 2021. Au was also an organizer of Macao's commemoration of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
Au said that he entered politics because he saw many social problems in daily life that required people to speak out. He said that the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement in 1989 brought him and his like-minded friends together, and he later felt Macao needed people to push forward an open and democratic society.
Before his arrest, Au was a rare voice in Macao who regularly criticized government measures and political developments on Facebook and in interviews, although many considered his critiques to be mild.
But the Macao government supported the ruling, urging all sectors to respect it. It said that the government would continue to strictly enforce the security law.
Beijing's Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office said that the ruling demonstrated Macao's firm resolve in safeguarding national security. It said that the ruling also reminded people to remain vigilant about the risks even in times of stability.
China's Foreign Ministry said that it firmly opposes any external forces using individual cases as a pretext to interfere in Macao's affairs.

articles.title_orig: Trump says 'big, beautiful' Russia-Ukraine deal in the works after meeting Putin's envoy
articles.title_zh: Trump says 'big, beautiful' Russia-Ukraine deal in the works after meeting Putin's envoy
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump on Thursday said a "very big" deal is in the works with Russia to end the Ukraine war.
Trump made the comments after he had an unscheduled meeting with Russian ⁠President Vladimir Putin's special envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House.
Speaking to ​reporters later, the president said the Russia-Ukraine war was ​very close to being settled and that bringing it to an end might involve "all of Europe."
"I can't tell you what I discussed. But I'm just telling you, it's going to be an agreement, it's going to be a big agreement," Trump said in the Oval Office.
"It's going to be very big. It's going to involve more than Ukraine , and I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."
Trump said he had not met with Ukrainian officials who were also at the White House on Thursday.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Meanwhile, Trump's son-in-law and US envoy Jared Kushner said the United States, NATO, ⁠and European ⁠partners held ​"productive and substantive ​discussions" on resolving ​the war in Ukraine Thursday.
"Our objective is to address the security concerns of all sides through practical, mutually agreed arrangements that reduce the risk of future conflict," he wrote on X, ​ahead of ⁠discussions ​next ​week in ​Abu Dhabi involving Kyiv and ​Moscow.
Even before his return to the White House, Trump has made similar promises regarding an imminent end to the conflict, famously saying he would end the war in one day upon becoming president.
Delegations from both Russia and Ukraine were at the White House on Thursday for an event honoring First Lady Melania Trump's work brokering a recent ceasefire in the war-ravaged city of Oleshky.
Speaking at her invitation, Russian envoy Dmitriev thanked the first lady for her "distinguished humanitarian role" in securing the six-day truce.
Dmitriev added that Putin personally gave instructions as part of the operation and sent his thanks to Melania Trump.
The head of the parliamentary faction of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's party, Davyd Arakhamia, and Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also spoke at the event.
Arakhamia told the first lady she did an "amazing job" and encouraged her to keep helping the Ukrainian people.
"Definitely we would like to ask you to keep going and to find new missions and to de-escalate more as much as possible," Arakhamia said.
