articles.title_orig: Small retailers brace for 'huge hit' this holiday season as shipping costs spike
articles.title_zh: Small retailers brace for 'huge hit' this holiday season as shipping costs spike
articles.content_orig:
When Jenni Shields began her small business eight years ago selling handmade hair accessories, she paid $2.93 to ship an order, or close to $4 in today's dollars when adjusted for inflation.
Last year, Shields said, an average shipping label for her products cost around $4.50. But when she took a typical batch of orders to her local U.S. Postal Service office last month in Kansas City, Kansas, she was shocked to see that it was an average of nearly $6 per package.
Shields is just one of the small- and medium-sized retailers who are struggling to keep up with rising shipping costs as the price of fuel continues to trend upward.
Small business owners such as Shields are facing a difficult holiday season. Customer demand is strong, but some retailers said their profits will be dented — if not eaten up entirely — by higher shipping and other costs.
Shields said she charges her customers $6 in shipping fees, which includes roughly $1.50 to cover her packaging supplies. The dramatic upswing this year means she's no longer breaking even on her orders and instead eating the added costs, she said.
"I am losing money at this point, and I've really taken a huge hit this year," said Shields, the owner of Evie Pearl Handmade, which sells bows, quilted headbands and other accessories. "I feel like it's just been this slow increase up [in shipping costs], and I feel horrible."
The surge in fuel prices since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February has driven up the cost of shipping by sea, air, rail and road.
That means higher costs across the board, including for shipping giant Amazon , which reported an 11% increase in shipping expenses in the third quarter compared with last year, to individual retailers.
Globally, air cargo is going for about $3.37 per kilogram, up 43% from a similar period a year ago, according to transportation marketplace Freightos. Judah Levine, Freightos' head of research, said in addition to higher fuel, demand for fast shipping of hardware used to build data centers is helping to boost air freight rates, even weeks before peak last-minute holiday packages take to the skies.
For businesses, that runup is going to "squeeze their margins in the near-term," said Jason Seidl, managing director and transportation analyst at TD Cowen. "Larger companies tend not to be exposed to the spot market, and they'll have what we call dedicated deals in place."
But that doesn't help smaller companies, which are walking a delicate line of not wanting to alienate customers who have enjoyed free shipping for nearly a generation.
Todd Shelton, founder of the eponymous 23-year-old New Jersey clothing company that makes high-end men's jeans, T-shirts and button-up shirts locally, said he started charging customers for return shipping this week for the first time after absorbing the higher expenses this year. The shipping is deducted from customers' refunds.
Shelton said his costs have been rising for materials, too, such as his imported Japanese denim and shirt fabric from Portugal. The company is still profitable, but the higher costs have eaten into profit margins as they stay elevated, he's considering raising prices or charging for shipping to customers, he said.
Shields said she's considering raising her shipping fees for the first time in six years to keep up with the increases.
The holiday season is one of Shields' busiest. But she said she's seen a slowdown in sales because of shipping fees.
"I can't compete with Amazon on the free shipping. I can't do that. I can't afford that," she said. "I'm seeing so much of my percentage that's supposed to come back to me and my family being put towards the shipping costs."
With no sign of fuel prices declining significantly, Shields, who runs her business out of her spare bedroom at home, said she's not sure that small businesses will be able to emerge on the other side of the holidays.
Shippers including UPS , FedEx and USPS have all instituted holiday surcharges, with prices varying by package type and lasting through the end of the season. Though that's typical during the peak holiday period each year, those charges have continued to rise over the past few years.
But even as costs everywhere climb, consumers are still spending.
According to the National Retail Federation , retail sales through the end of the year are expected to grow 4.2%, translating to total spending of $1.01 trillion. That's compared with last year's holiday sales totaling $972 billion, which was 3.1% growth.
Some of that growth is from inflation , meaning consumers are simply paying more for the same goods.
"Customers all expect to spend more this holiday, but part of why they expect to spend more is they expect things to cost more, not because they'd like to spend more or they were hoping to get more quantity of stuff," said Aaron Cheris, the global retail practice head at Bain & Company. "So what I suspect happens is that non-discretionary categories do fine, because you buy the food you were going to need to buy anyway, but then the amount of cash that's left over for [discretionary] goods is less."
Still, Cheris said it's shaping up to be a record year for shipping costs, which is putting immense pressure on smaller retailers. That means many retailers may find themselves in financial distress in the first quarter of next year as they struggle to make it through the holiday season.
He added that larger retail companies will also have to reckon with rising costs, though they may not feel those effects until later quarters because they have shipping contracts that have already been locked in and have control over their own delivery fleets.
"If anything, it benefits the scale players over the little players, but it's kind of a little bit bad for everybody," Cheris said. "I think that is the challenge."

articles.title_orig: Why gold prices are surprisingly low : Planet Money
articles.title_zh: Why gold prices are surprisingly low : Planet Money
articles.content_orig:
You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
Scammers can even make money off of people starved for FAN fiction. That's my takeaway from a fake website popping up that tried to sell computer-generated audiobooks of fan fiction, which is content created by ANYONE based off of existing works. "Fifty Shades of Grey" started as a fanfic of Twilight, for example.
This scam website popped up in the wake of the uber-popular fan fiction website AO3 , Archive of our Own, going down for an estimated two to four weeks after a "security incident." People are starved for their stories and apparently will click on anything. Lucky for the world, the scam website has been taken down .
What to know: North Korea just loves stealing crypto. They love it! It's become a major part of their economy. Last week, a state-sponsored hacking group called "TraderTraitor" executed the largest crypto theft in history, stealing $6.43 billion from Binance, a massive cryptocurrency exchange. $2.85 billion has been frozen or seized, according to Elliptic , a crypto analytics & compliance firm. But $3.35 billion is still linked to the group. "TraderTraitor" is actively trying to launder this money (yes, crypto is surprisingly traceable). A huge part of the stolen funds are in stablecoin, which can be frozen. Whatever isn't already frozen, the hacking group is trying to launder it and FAST. So how are they doing it?
"TraderTraitor" is trying to quickly turn Stablecoin into Ether, a harder to freeze crypto PETER PARKS/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption
How are the criminals laundering these assets?: Laundering this much crypto is NOT simple. The intelligence firm Elliptic broke down how "TraderTraitor" is trying to quickly protect its newfound loot. First of all, they want to turn any Stablecoin into assets that cannot be frozen, like Ether (ETH). From there, the group is using automation to create LOTS of new wallets to filter small amounts of crypto, so as not to trigger alarms for moving assets worth a bazillion dollars. From there, launderers want to move the money across networks like Ethereum to Bitcoin then pull it from a mixed pool with a bunch of other people's assets. The goal: make the crypto's origins hazy. "TraderTraitor" is moving fast. On Tuesday, Elliptic reported the group has made more than 40,000 transactions, creating a new wallet every 25 seconds.
One interesting detail: Binance has promised to make customers whole , but investors have already pulled billions from the exchange.
What to know: This week, gold fell below $4,000 per ounce after hitting nearly $5,600 per ounce in January. It's typically seen as a safe-haven asset, which is why investors were shoveling money into it earlier this year. As you know, things have been a bit volatile from the Iran War to the criminal probe into the Federal Reserve chair. But today, there's still economic uncertainty, no? The war with Iran rages on. So why are gold prices falling? I took my question to Planet Money co-host Jeff Guo to find out. I asked him: could gold be going down because Treasury bond yields are up? That could mean there are MORE reliable ways to make money.
Why is gold going down? : Our answer, courtesy of Jeff Guo!
Jeff: I think you are right that rising Treasury yields are the story. As you know, gold tends to be seen as a "safe" asset and an inflation hedge; but the problem is that gold doesn't earn any income/interest on its own. Meanwhile, you could buy a 10 year TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) bond right now that does earn income, above and beyond inflation. Sure, the Iran war is a source of political instability that might drive investors toward gold. But the main effect of the war so far seems to be raising the price of oil. And higher oil prices are one of the factors pushing interest rates up, making bonds more attractive relative to gold.
What to know: People do not want data centers and the election left us with numbers to prove it. Apparently voters either BANNED or placed restrictions on data centers in at least 38 jurisdictions across the country. The numbers within the ballot measures were fascinating. It's also notable that Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, ran on a platform of reining in data centers. She called for a moratorium on new projects and pushing for more aggressive protections on both ratepayers and the environment. A Democrat hasn't been governor in Texas in more than 30 years.
Why it matters: All this local opposition could actually make an impact on what big tech wants to do. Local opposition has already made a difference in data center world. S&P Global has tracked projects nationwide and found more than 146 were delayed or canceled through early August. 75% of those were tied to local opposition. Several big tech companies are dropping contract provisions that have drawn the public's ire – one that keeps early phases of data center projects a secret, for example. We will be keeping an eye on this.
If you're buying a house, you have a choice on what kind of mortgage to get. The "fixed-rate" mortgage has become dominant in the U.S. The "adjustable-rate" mortgage (ARM) makes up only five percent of mortgages here. They used to be much more popular until the 2008 financial crisis showed adjustable rates can be risky! In 2008, a man in Colorado saw his interest rate rise to NINE percent. He and his wife owed more than the house was worth.
" I am on the Titanic, watching it sink I don't even have a lifeboat," he told NPR at the time.
But now, the adjustable-rate mortgage is rising in popularity again. They represented 11% of new mortgage applications, the highest in more than a year. What's going on?
LISTEN TO THE FULL EPISODE
The origins of this story: The show Planet Money was actually born out of a collaborative story between NPR and This American Life called The Giant Pool of Money explaining the 2008 financial crisis. The episode moves through the housing crash by following a chain of people relevant to the market collapsing. It includes a guy (not the Colorado guy) who took out an adjustable-rate mortgage and things did NOT end well for him. His mortgage rate adjusted upwards by more than $2,000 per month due to his adjustable rate.

Producer Angel Carreras is reading DC's Absolute Martian Manhunter
I swear I read real books and NBER [National Bureau of Economic Research] papers, but I must recommend another comic: DC's Absolute Martian Manhunter.
Instead of the cartoon alien who loves Oreos and beats up other alien bad guys, this run turns John Jones (FKA J'onn J'onnz) into an FBI agent who survives a suicide bombing and merges with an alien entity. What follows is a psychedelic, politically charged comic, one that's deeply attuned to modern anxieties from the police state and climate dread to the slow erosion of the social contract and xenophobia.
Sounds heavy, but it's so wildly inventive with the medium (hold this page up to the sun! cut these bits out of the next page!) that you won't be able to put it down.

articles.title_orig: The Enough Phone is made by and for people fed up with big screens
articles.title_zh: The Enough Phone is made by and for people fed up with big screens
articles.content_orig:
It’s a little phone with a big challenge ahead of it.
It’s a little phone with a big challenge ahead of it.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
It’s a bad time and maybe also a great time to make a new smartphone.
Brennan Jordan and Austin Boer are two-thirds of the trio behind the Enough Phone , a small phone that will run your choice of stock Android or the minimalist OdysseyOS. They’re currently seeking funding on Kickstarter , and just a day after launching, the project is over halfway to its $250,000 goal.
The Enough Phone’s target specifications include a 5.3-inch display, 3,500mAh user-replaceable battery, MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chipset, a 50-megapixel Sony sensor in the rear camera, and 8GB of RAM. The dimensions listed on the Kickstarter page suggest an iPhone Mini-ish size; Jordan and Boer also happen to be former iPhone Mini users themselves.
The two of them cofounded a software startup called Sleke , which sells refurbished phones loaded with OdysseyOS, their minimalist, low-distraction version of Android. Putting the software on existing phones is a win for sustainability, but it also helps them get their software to market faster, Boer tells me. The pair offers small batches of Pixel 8 and 9 phones right now through the Sleke website, but the large devices didn’t feel quite right to some customers.
“One of the biggest things that we get is, ‘I don’t want this large of a phone for a minimal operating system,’” says Boer. They’d wanted to make a small phone, and the opportunity arrived when Will Stults approached them about creating one. Stults operates an online store for non-smartphones called Dumbwireless . He also brings familiarity with the smartphone manufacturing process to the mix thanks to some previous work with a “big” phone brand.
But hardware is hard in the best of times, and 2026 has proven extremely challenging for phone companies big and small. The chip shortage has driven prices up and made RAM scarce. Jordan and Boer are feeling the pressures, particularly around pricing. The Kickstarter campaign offers some discounts for early backers, but after that the Enough Phone will sell for $599. “We don’t want to be charging as much as we are,” says Boer, “but as a startup you can only do so much.” They’re a self-funded operation and want to keep it that way, he says, so they can choose their own priorities. Outside funding would change the dynamic and might put pressure on them to shorten their promised five years of software support or cut other costs.
As it stands, the project is on schedule. According to the Kickstarter page, it’s in the production tooling phase, with plans to ship phones to customers in May 2027 — though a footnote says that the RAM shortage’s “ripple effects across the entire electronics manufacturing industry” could still throw a wrench in the works.
Prospects for small phone fans (disclosure: I am one ) were bleak even before the chip crisis. Apple’s last Mini was released five years ago, and there’s no indication of another one in sight. Asus’ Zenfone used to be a nice, small-ish Android option before the company made it bigger and quit selling it in the US . Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky made a lot of noise about launching a small phone, but has since shifted priorities . And there’s Unihertz’s Jelly Max — certainly small, but its specs lag behind a modern midrange phone.
Boer sees this gap as an opportunity, even in the midst of a global RAM crisis. “Nobody was doing it, and we’re kind of seeing why — because it’s not the ideal time to start. But that also kind of makes it the ideal time to start, because no one else is doing it,” he says. “Let’s just do it ourselves.” Enough is enough. At least that’s what they’re hoping.

articles.title_orig: After printing 40,000 whistles, this is the 3D printer I’d buy
articles.title_zh: After printing 40,000 whistles, this is the 3D printer I’d buy
articles.content_orig:
One year later, the Bambu P2S Combo is the only 3D printer I can easily recommend.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
I’ve been wanting to try 3D printing , people tell me. Which printer should I get?
I finally have a fairly easy answer: the Bambu Lab P2S Combo . The auto-loading, fully enclosed touchscreen printer is one of the very few I can recommend. It’s the only one I’d buy for myself. It’s on sale for $649 through December 1st, but I’d vouch for it even at its normal $749 price.
I’ve spent an entire year testing the P2S alongside several competitors, printing 40,000 whistles for ICE whistleblowers along the way. After racking up 6,770 hours of print time across four different printers, I’m sure of my recommendation.
Some people who know 3D printers will argue with me:
But for the reasons I’ll explain below, the P2S Combo is my pick despite all of that. It’s durable, reliable, and simple to maintain and clean and forget about, even in ways my trusty Bambu P1P and the similar P1S lacked.
The P2S makes 3D printing easy. When I’m in the mood, I don’t even need to walk over to my printer half the time. I can fire it up from my phone or laptop, using Bambu’s app to send one of millions of ready-made models from the cloud. The automated material system (AMS) automatically loads one of the rolls of filament that I leave in its protected enclosure for months at at time without fear. It automatically calibrates, automatically prints, automatically winds the filament back up when it’s done.
I tell friends that no matter which printer you buy, you should buy a multi-material system “Combo” because manually loading and unloading filament is a chore; it means standing around a printer waiting for it to heat up and feeding plastic into a tube by hand. Automated filament systems can fix that. For me, it’s not about having lots of colors in a single print; it’s about knowing I can print something black, or white, or red, or my kid’s favorite sparkly purple without any further effort — because I loaded those colors weeks ago.
It is true that the $369 Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo also has automatic four-color filament feeding at a seemingly unbeatable price, and printed whistles and household items just as well as the P2S. I’ve spent 1,271 hours printing with the Centauri Carbon, and 939 hours with a Centauri Carbon 2, and they printed almost flawlessly right out of the box — no need to level a bed, no need to adjust belt tension, the printer calibrates itself.
But like other Bambu rivals, Elegoo doesn’t automatically load its filament from mostly airtight containers. I can’t leave rolls of filament in the printer for weeks or months when I’m not actively using them because they’ll quickly absorb moisture from the air, turn brittle, and jam up the printer’s tubes or nozzle.
Moisture is the primary reason I wouldn’t recommend an inexpensive Bambu A1 Combo to newcomers, either, or a Snapmaker U1, or any other attractive multicolor printer without sealed filament storage. The entire experience of using a 3D printer is friendlier when you don’t have to prep the printer before printing.
Even so, it’s pretty dang tempting to save $280 or more by going with the Elegoo. But over the course of the roughly 1,000 hours I tested the Carbon and Carbon 2 side by side with the Bambu P2S, the Elegoo printers broke down in ways that were more difficult to diagnose.
The original Carbon’s extruder had some feeding issues and I found a lot of black dust inside after taking it apart, seemingly from worn plastic gears. Just this week, my Carbon 2’s stopped working after its nozzle mysteriously crashed into the bed and it refused to auto-level itself (which would normally fix that issue). I had to take the bed apart and still couldn’t find anything wrong.
In the end, yanking and reseating four tiny fragile-and-yet-too-tight connectors inside the bed fixed that problem, but it’s not the kind of solution a consumer should have to do.
Anecdotally, my Bambu printers have led a comparatively charmed life: In 1,692 hours of printing with the P2S, I’ve had to swap out the nozzle twice, clean and relubricate the traversal rods and screws several times, wash the removable magnetic printing surfaces a bunch of times with water and dish soap, and clear several filament jams in the AMS. That’s about it.
P2S nozzle replacements are easier, too. When you jam today’s Elegoo printers, you’re going old-school, either by wrenching off a hot nozzle so you can clean or inexpensively replace it ($25 for eight nozzles) or by fishing out tiny wires and unscrewing two bolts to remove an entire $30 hotend (which includes the elements that heat the plastic) at once. With Bambu’s P2S, you can just yank off a gasket and open one spring clip to swap a whole new toolless hotend ($18) in less than a minute. It does help to have a pair of mini pliers to grab the nozzle, though.
The Elegoo printers also have noisy fans that stay active even when you’re not printing, unlike the Bambu, though the Centauri Carbon 2 does shut them off more quickly than the original. Both Elegoo and Bambu let you remotely monitor your prints from its built-in camera and capture timelapse videos, but Elegoo’s camera and lighting are crap quality by comparison.
If I’m being completely honest, Bambu’s own Bambu P1S Combo, at $509 on sale , is the closest competition for the $649 P2S Combo, and I had a hunch it might be my pick in the end. I upgraded my P1P with most of the P1S upgrades, and it’s been a reliable workhorse: nearly 3,000 hours of 3D printing so far.
But over the past year, I’ve gravitated towards the P2S more and more because of its easy-swap hotends, the built-in touchscreen where I easily manage prints and rolls of filament, and all kinds of little improvements that I find I actually care about:
Plus, I did have to replace the entire heatbed on my P1P once. I can’t say that nothing will go wrong with the P2S, and you shouldn’t take away that they’re as simple as an inkjet. They will need occasional maintenance, you’ll need to load good-quality filament and probably want to avoid rolls that come on lightweight cardboard (I try to buy Bambu, Sunlu, or Elegoo refills for my reusable plastic Bambu spools), and even then there will be components that wear out.
After 1,600 hours, the AMS 2 that came with my Bambu P2S review unit sometimes complains when trying to unwind or rewind some rolls of filament from some slots, and I suspect it’s because some of the gears are wearing prematurely. Bambu recently announced it’ll replace some of those gears free of charge, but only ones manufactured between May and July 2026, and even then you’ll have to be pretty handy to install them yourself .
I strongly believe people buying their first printer should get something tried and true, fully baked, simple to use, and the P2S is the best yet. But even Bambu is still catering more to DIY enthusiasts who’ll tolerate the occasional hardware defect.
So yes, if you’re asking “Which printer should I get,” I think you’d be pleasantly surprised with a P2S! But I wouldn’t blame you for waiting a few more years.

articles.title_orig: Grim details emerge after woman and daughter killed by suspected grizzly bear in Canada
articles.title_zh: Grim details emerge after woman and daughter killed by suspected grizzly bear in Canada
articles.content_orig:
Selah Reed's family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister.
When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia's central coast. Balcarras' car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found.
Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras' brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly.
When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found . The search was now a tragic recovery effort.
The killings of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 3 to 4 kilometers (1.8 to 2.4 miles) from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack.
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials have set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend's attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. They also are not sure whether more than one bear was involved.
Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said the killings were triggering for the families who were traumatized by last year's attack.
"Our community is still healing," he said, adding that they've imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. "Our priority is to ensure they're safe and ensure our community is supported."
The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain, even though it was close to the trailhead, and the grizzly bear's behavior.
Searchers found Jenny Balcarras first, then her daughter. The search was helped by more resources and a cadaver dog, Matt Balcarras said.
Searchers found his niece's remains in a bear cache - a place where bears stash food, sometimes by digging a small hole and covering it with branches and vegetation to keep other animals and birds away.
"Even though it was within 100 or so meters (330 feet), locating remains in a cache is difficult," he said.
By the time officials located his niece, she could only be identified by her clothing, he said. His sister was in a similar condition, but they knew who she was thanks to several tiny tattoos, he said.
"There's no obvious body to identify," he said. "The coroner's investigation will include DNA and dental work. But there is no doubt that the remains that were found are theirs."
Grizzly bears are common in the area surrounding the Bella Coola community, officials said. Conservation officials maintain a hotline where people can report problem bears, but no calls had been received recently, Tyre said during a media briefing.
Balcarras, an art therapist, had moved to Bella Coola during the summer. She had previously lived in Alaska, where her children were born, and was "the central organizing person in our family," Matt Balcarras said.
"In classic, strong single-mother style, she scraped together a career and a life for herself and her kids," Balcarras said. She was small in stature but strong in character and physical abilities, he said.
She was comfortable living among the wildlife, he said.
"She lived in the Bush when her kids were babies," he said. "She and my niece were not naive or foolish or uninformed. They've lived in these areas and have been around animals of countless types for years and years and decades."
There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks . The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.
In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.
A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.
A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.
Ahmad  Mukhtar contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Retail traders dump $257 million in stocks in 5th biggest selling day since 2020
articles.title_zh: Retail traders dump $257 million in stocks in 5th biggest selling day since 2020
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Retail investors dumped US stocks on Thursday at a pace not seen since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, breaking with their typical market-down-day habit of "buying the dip."
Everyday investors sold a net $257 million in individual US stocks on Thursday, according to Vanda Research, the fifth biggest single-day of net selling spree since March 17, 2020, when retail investors pulled $502 million from individual stocks.
"This is what we would call a total capitulation by retail investors," Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda Research, said in emailed comments.
US stocks plunged on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday's post-election rally. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 5.2%, putting the index on track to close in a correction.
Retail selling marks something of a departure from a tendency by individual investors in recent years to scoop up shares when markets tumble. Vanda said there were "no signs of buying the dip" in individual stocks, though some investors continued to purchase leveraged exchange-traded funds such as ProShares UltraPro QQQ ( TQQQ ) and Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares ( SOXL ).
Vanda added that net selling was a third higher earlier Thursday afternoon before late "late-session" retail buyers stepped in
Patel added that the retreat echoed a broader "buyers' strike" among institutional investors alongside forced selling by systematic and leveraged investment strategies.
Story updated with Vanda Research end of day data.

articles.title_zh: Beijing approves giant Long March 9 rocket for deep-space and lunar base runs
articles.content_orig:
Maiden flight is set for 2030, with ground construction already under way at Hainan’s Wenchang assembly complex
The stainless-steel giant received official approval last month, according to the slide. At 110 metres (361 feet) tall and 10.6 metres wide, it will be the most powerful and expensive launcher China has ever built.
The slide, presented in the northwestern city of Xian by a researcher from the country’s main state-owned rocket maker, shows the Long March 9 is set to make its maiden flight in 2030. It will haul big loads to the moon and Mars, and help build solar power stations in space.
Its first stage will be powered by 30 methane-burning engines, producing about 6,000 tonnes of thrust at lift-off. On lunar missions, the rocket will be able to carry 50 tonnes – about the weight of eight elephants.

articles.title_orig: Bomb threats continue to target aircrafts across Europe
articles.title_zh: Bomb threats continue to target aircrafts across Europe
articles.content_orig:
A string of bomb threats continued to target flights across Europe on Friday.
A Ryanair flight travelling from Rome to Lisbon was placed under a security alert after an anonymous phone call to the control tower at Rome’s Fiumicino Airport warned of a possible explosive device on board, according to reports.
The aircraft landed at Lisbon's Humberto Delgado Airport shortly before 8 am. Authorities are investigating the threat, but there has been no confirmation of explosives on board.
Meanwhile, the French Prime Minister's office declared that there had been four more bomb alerts concerning "planes flying over French territory" on Friday morning.
"The aircrafts landed safely. Security services are conducting inspections", said the PM's office, while adding that "an investigation is underway to determine the source of these alerts, which are affecting the whole of Europe."
Concerning the Rome-Lisbon flight, CNN Portugal reported that Portugal's Public Security Police (PSP) received a telephone call from a person described as a "law enforcement officer", warning of a possible explosive device on board. The caller's identity was reportedly verified by the Judicial Police (PJ).
When contacted by Euronews, Lisbon Airport referred enquiries to the PSP, which has not yet confirmed the reported incident. Euronews also attempted to contact the PJ but has not received a response.
Another bomb alert was reported on a Wizz Air flight travelling from Prague to Rome. The aircraft was diverted to Venice, where it landed.
The latest incidents follow a wave of bomb scares that affected at least 25 flights across Europe on Thursday. EU officials have said it is too early to determine whether the incidents are linked.

articles.title_orig: JLR marks nine consecutive years at CIIE, reaffirming commitment to China
articles.title_zh: JLR marks nine consecutive years at CIIE, reaffirming commitment to China
articles.content_orig:
Jaguar Land Rover, the first British automotive manufacturer to exhibit at the China International Import Expo, marks its ninth consecutive year at the expo, affirming its confidence in the Chinese market, as well as its continued investment and deepening engagement in China.
As the ninth CIIE, which opened in Shanghai on Nov 5, the United Kingdom's largest automotive manufacturer JLR is presenting seven distinctive vehicles, a Range Rover SV Bespoke experience and its corporate social responsibility initiatives in the Automobile and Smart Mobility exhibition zone in Hall 7.2.
Tim Howard, CEO of JLR China, said that "CIIE brings us closer to Chinese clients and partners, giving us firsthand insight into the dynamism and openness of the market. Looking ahead, we will continue to broaden our product portfolio, create distinctive brand experiences and enhance support throughout the client journey, translating the insights gained at CIIE into sustainable performance and long-term value."
Kate Harrisson, His Majesty's trade commissioner for the Chinese mainland and Hong Kong, visited the JLR booth. She said "JLR is a strong example of a British company investing in China and working pragmatically with Chinese partners. Its participation in CIIE for nine consecutive years reflects its sustained commitment to the market, while showcasing British strengths in engineering, innovation and responsible business."
"There is significant scope for closer UK-China collaboration in advanced manufacturing, the green transition and trade in services," she said, adding that "We look forward to JLR continuing to act as a bridge and helping to foster practical, mutually beneficial partnerships between British and Chinese businesses."
On the opening day, Li Guoqing, deputy director-general of the China International Import Expo Bureau, presented JLR with a commemorative award recognizing its participation in all nine editions of CIIE.
"CIIE is a key platform for China to pursue high-standard opening-up and promote global cooperation, and has always been committed to creating an open platform for international cooperation. We look forward to JLR continuing to use CIIE as a platform to share in China's development opportunities and create long-term value," Li said.
At this year's CIIE, JLR is presenting seven vehicles from the Range Rover and Defender brands. Among the exhibits is a classic Land Rover Series I, built in 1955, which completed the first overland crossing of Eurasia. It represents an early expression of the reliability, durability and spirit of exploration that continue to define Defender today.

The design of the protective shell uses low-density plywood formed into a smooth aerodynamic curve, supported by an internal metal framework to bear loads, according to the Jiangsu-based company.

articles.title_orig: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.title_zh: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.content_orig:
Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday.
“Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA).
Iran effectively shut the strait early in the US-Israel war on Iran , which began on February 28, and the United States reimposed a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.
So why have these four countries been granted passage through the critical strait, and can their ships really sail freely while the blockade remains in place?
It will receive medicine from India and political backing from China, according to Hayat Moqaddam. Iran already receives diplomatic support from Qatar, which is leading mediation efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hayat Moqaddam said Tehran will also collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships, while Qatari vessels pass free. He did not say whether Iraqi ships will pay a toll.
“Whatever the lawmaker says is the rationale – the big question is if it works and, if yes, to what extent?” Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.
“Iran has been under sanctions for a very long time, so bartering and quid pro quos in trade are nothing new,” he said. The difference now, he added, is that “it’s about poking holes in an embargo and getting crucial goods/services in and out”.
Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, said that “most likely Iran is charging a transit fee or a percentage of the cargo value to allow those ships to go through without being harassed”.
“It’s a clever move by Tehran for several reasons,” Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, told Al Jazeera.
“If successful, this move will generate significant revenue for Iran, as China is by far the largest purchaser of Iranian crude oil, buying nearly 90 percent of Iran’s total oil exports,” he said.
By including Qatar, with its many liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers, and India, Iran is also “trying to undermine acceptance” of Washington’s strategy in the conflict, especially as it charges Qatar no tolls, he added.
All four are highly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for exports.
Of the 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
“China is the country most able to cross US interests. The question is whether Beijing considers it worth the potential political cost,” Parsi said.
Asia is particularly reliant on Gulf oil and gas usually shipped out via Hormuz. Countries there have much to offer in return for allowing ships to pass.
“For India, the shutdown of oil from the Gulf has been a great loss – and it is a big producer of the pharmaceuticals that Iran cannot manufacture itself,” he said.
Qatar, which is mediating between Washington and Tehran, shipped no LNG through the strait in August, but managed 1.8 million tonnes in October, Xu said.
Its crude transits fell over the same period, from 517,000 barrels a day to 193,000, while Iraq’s rose from 1.69 million to 2.65 million.
Kpler has been unable to trace the origin of up to two million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, so both countries’ flows may be higher, Xu said.
“India and Qatar have closer relationships with DC they need to maintain – while both of them also feel let down by Trump,” Parsi said, adding, “For Qatar, maintaining a relationship with Iran is also vital since it’s an unavoidable neighbour.”
“So for all of them, there are upsides for these exemptions from Iranian restrictions but also political dangers,” he said.
Iran began letting some vessels from countries it considers friendly pass within weeks of the war starting. And in April, its military command said “brotherly” Iraq was exempt.
With the Iraqi exemption, Iran “probably intends to support the economic recovery” of its western neighbour, a fellow Shia-majority country, Pusztai said.
That depends on Washington.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said the blockade applies to “all vessels of all nations entering or leaving coastal areas or ports in Iran”, while vessels avoiding Iranian ports are not affected.
It has also said humanitarian shipments, including “food and medical supplies essential for the survival of the civilian populations”, can pass after inspection.
But Hayat Moqaddam did not appear to limit the exemptions to ships trading with other Gulf states, Pusztai noted. “If this is really the case, this would also have a significant impact on the other Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia,” he said.
“This could make the continuation of the American naval blockade more difficult and less effective, assuming Washington accepts this Iranian move,” he said. The main change, he added, is that the exemption “would also cover Chinese/Indian ships from/to Iran”, if the US accepts it.
It is also unclear whether “ships of these countries” means the flag a vessel flies, its owner, its operator or some other link, Pusztai said.
Ending the blockade is one of Tehran’s demands before it will commit to broader peace talks with the US, which will include discussions about Iran’s nuclear programme. Qatar-mediated talks currently centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait if the US meets seven conditions, including this and lifting sanctions.
“It seems to be that Iran tries to separate the questions of free passage through the Strait of Hormuz and oil exports from the nuclear question,” Pusztai said, adding, “The American reaction will show if this is successful.”
“I think they make only limited difference at present,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.
“Markets are back to pricing in a peace deal, but if conflict flares up at full tilt, then Iranian commanders may not have time to distinguish their targets,” he said, adding: “At present, the focus remains squarely on the prospects of a broader deal.”
An exemption has not guaranteed safety. On October 30, the Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck by “unidentified objects” in the Gulf, said its owner, Qatar Gas Transport Company.
More than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, with October being the worst month, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.

articles.title_orig: Japan’s Nikkei Breaks Below Key 60,000 Level on AI Selloff
articles.title_zh: Japan’s Nikkei Breaks Below Key 60,000 Level on AI Selloff
articles.content_orig:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news, as Asia-Pacific markets slide after Wall Street rout
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
Fears that the Democratic Party’s blue wave in this week’s midterm elections will sink the AI investment boom are roiling markets, following heavy losses on Wall Street last night.
Asia-Pacific markets are a sea of red (unlike the US election map on Tuesday night!), as investors ditch tech stocks after more than $3.2tn was wiped off the US stock market yesterday.
Today, Japan’s Nikkei stock index has slumped by almost 6% – its worst drop since April 7 2025 during the ‘liberation day’ tariff panic.
South Korea’s KOSPI is down 6.7%, and Taiwan’s TAIEX has dropped by 4.5% in a broad rout.
Christopher Forbes , head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets , called the market action “a bit of a disaster”, explaining ( via Reuters ):
double quotation mark “(Clients) were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out.
“All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints, ... because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome and you’re telling them, look, you’ve just lost money.
“And it’s not just a slap in terms of valuation. It’s basically a whole policy and six-year structural shift that says we’re now going to pause, we’re now going to cool AI, we’re now going to cool data centres, approvals and equity capital markets.”
After months of warnings that AI valuations were too high, and that the bubble might burst, US investors dashed to the exits en masse yesterday. The Nasdaq tech index slumped by 5.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and the S&P 500 lost 4.36%.
Memory chip makers, who had been profiting from the AI boom, led the fallers – SanDisk slumped 22% and both Micron and AMD lost 17% of their value.
Chip giant Nvidia led the fallers on the DJIA , down over 9%.
Analysts pointed to policy uncertainty as Democrats are more critical of data centres, which could slow the rollout of AI investment – especially given public opposition to the sector .
Kyle Rodda , senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, says it was a “brutal sell-off” as fears about the future of the AI buildout gripped the markets.
double quotation mark The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom.
The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations. Earnings season has been an overall disappointment for the markets, with Magnificent Seven results so far undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down.
So, it could be a ‘tin hats on’ day in the markets. Investors will also be watching the latest US jobs report, for clues into the health of America’s labour market.
7am GMT: Lloyds house price index
9am GMT: UN’s FAO food price index
1.30pm GMT: US non-farm payrolls jobs report
3pm GMT: University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence report
Interestingly, Jefferies economist Mohit Kumar doesn’t believe yesterday’s losses are “the start of the unwind of the AI trade”.
double quotation mark We do admit that policy uncertainty after the Blue Tsunami raises concerns over AI investment and the pace of data center buildup.
However, data centers and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move onto other states or outside the country. AI investment has been a key driver of US growth, and we do not see Democrats as giving up on this growth engine.
There was a huge slump in the most AI-exposed parts of the US stock market yesterday, Jim Reid of Deutche Bank told clients this morning:
double quotation mark In fact, the scale of the moves ranked among the biggest in years, and the Philly semiconductor index (-12.25%) had its worst day since the pandemic slump in March 2020 . And in turn, that cascaded elsewhere, with the S&P 500 (-4.36%) posting its biggest slump since the Liberation Day volatility in April 2025 .
So that drove a huge surge in the VIX index (+11.6pts), which also saw its biggest daily jump since the Liberation Day period, ending the session at 28.2pts, its highest since March.
Mohit Kumar, economist at investent bank Jefferies , doesn’t expect a quick rebound from yesterday’s losses.
double quotation mark In previous episodes of retail selling, institutional investors have stepped in to find value. The approaching year-end complicates the behaviour of institutional accounts as risk appetite would be limited….
The geopolitical uncertainty around possible US action in Iran also suggests that investors would not rush to add risk.
Stuart Clark , portfolio manager at Quilter , points out that the dominance of the tech sector exacerbated yesterday’s selloff:
double quotation mark “The blue wave at the ballot box has quickly been replaced by a sea of red on investors’ screens. Technology stocks have sold off sharply, with the immediate catalyst appearing to be concerns around tougher AI regulation, covering both the models themselves and the vast data centre infrastructure required to support them.
“The scale of the falls in some of the market’s biggest names has been striking. But it also highlights the concentration risk that has built up in US equity markets. With a relatively small number of technology and semiconductor stocks now carrying so much weight, weakness in those names quickly translates into sizeable falls for the Nasdaq and S&P 500.
Ahead of this week’s losses, there were plenty of warning signs that markets might have risen too fast.
As my colleague Richard Partington and I wrote in late September, the warning lights were “flashing red” as the fighting in the Middle East intensified, a slowdown loomed in the AI arms race, and government borrowing costs hit multi-decade highs.
One popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE ratio – or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio – had risen to its highest level since 2000 by September, showing that the US stock market is unusually highly valued compared with its profits.
This week’s losses have pulled the CAPE ratio down ( you can see it here ), but it’s still historically high:
Amid the scary-everything-is-bad-in-stocks news, it’s easy to feel a bit worried about pensions or savings, my colleague Siraj Datoo writes.
And yes, yesterday was a bad day in particular for technology stocks, with the Nasdaq losing $2.5tn in market capital in a single day.
But it’s worth taking a second to pause. While many of the charts leading newspaper homepages are fairly narrow, showing the dramatic fall in just a few days, if you look at the Nasdaq, the US index mostly dominated by tech stocks, from the start of the year, it’s still up 4.6% YTD ( see previous post for more details ).
Of course, this correction still could have room to run and markets are famously emotional. But there have been warnings about this. Michael Burry, the famous fund manager behind The Big Short, has been screaming from the sidelines about overvaluations in the tech world.
One of the major concerns right now is the huge data centre buildout in the US and whether Democrats will place restrictions or slow things down. That’s a problem for investors because so many of the world’s biggest companies have invested enormous amounts of money -- often taking on additional debt -- to fund their deep investment. The bet is that the artificial buildout will eventually generate big returns but investors are now increasingly worried about just how long that will take.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay Congress rejects President Pena’s resignation after bank collapse
articles.title_zh: Paraguay Congress rejects President Pena’s resignation after bank collapse
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay’s Congress has refused to accept President Santiago Pena’s resignation, pressing ahead with impeachment proceedings after the collapse of digital lender Ueno Bank.
President since 2023, Pena had attempted to resign on Thursday as millions of Ueno customers remained unable to access their accounts.
“I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” the conservative politician said in a recorded address.
But lawmakers declined to accept his resignation. The lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, and the Senate opened impeachment proceedings, summoning him to appear on Friday.
A joint congressional session called to consider the resignation lost its quorum after lawmakers from Pena’s Colorado Party walked out, as it became clear there were not enough votes to accept it.
Horacio Cartes, a leader in the Colorado Party, had posted a statement on social media indicating the group supported Pena’s impeachment.
“We will not side with the theft of public, private and pension funds,” Cartes, a former president, wrote in his statement. “We must think of the people and the values we uphold in the Colorado Party.”
Denying Pena’s resignation is likely to heighten the legal jeopardy he faces.
Ordinarily, in Paraguay, presidents who leave office become senators for life, and they enjoy a degree of legal immunity from prosecution as members of the legislature.
But that status is not conferred if the president is convicted in an impeachment trial.
The political crisis erupted earlier this week, when Paraguay’s central bank announced that Ueno had fallen below the legal solvency ratio. Once its books were corrected, the bank’s capital – the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses – was less than half the legal minimum.
Before its collapse, the company claimed it had about 3 million customers, in a country of 6.5 million people. Many have since lost access to their accounts and to pensions paid out through the bank.
As part of a resolution to address the bank’s collapse, Paraguay’s central bank voted to transfer its remaining funds to other financial institutions.
But the central bank itself came under scrutiny for not properly regulating Ueno. The central bank’s head, Carlos Carvallo, has since resigned.
Pena himself formerly held a stake in Ueno’s parent company, Grupo Vazquez, though he said he sold those shares in 2025.
Lawmakers, however, have accused Pena of having a conflict of interest and have questioned whether there was an institutional cover-up linked to the lender’s collapse.
“He is accused of negligence at the very least and complicity in covering up the fact that the bank was insolvent,” said Al Jazeera’s Latin America editor Lucia Newman.
“As I speak, there are people outside urging Congress not to accept the resignation of the president because they say that they want him tried and impeached.”
Until its demise, Ueno had grown quickly from a niche company into a mid-tier bank administering close to $850m in public funds.
Paraguay’s attorney general has also ordered three criminal investigations into the bank’s collapse, which will look into oversight of the lender and the placement of public funds in the institution. Pena has said he will cooperate with investigators.
“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfil its purpose, and that public funds – as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans – be protected,” Pena added in his address.
If Pena is ultimately removed from office, Vice President Pedro Alliana would likely take over as president.
Ueno has made no public statement on the issue.

articles.title_orig: 12 Planes in 12 Days: Pope Begins Major Latin America Tour, Weeks After Surgery
articles.title_zh: 12 Planes in 12 Days: Pope Begins Major Latin America Tour, Weeks After Surgery
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title_orig: The IRS has announced new tax brackets for 2027: See where you land
articles.title_zh: The IRS has announced new tax brackets for 2027: See where you land
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new federal income tax brackets and standard deductions for 2027.
In its announcement Thursday, the agency raised the income thresholds for each bracket, which apply to tax year 2027 for returns filed in 2028.
The IRS also increased figures for other key provisions, including long-term capital gains brackets, the estate and gift tax exemption , and eligibility for the earned income tax credit, among others.
For 2027, the top rate of 37% applies to individuals with taxable income above $661,375 and married couples filing jointly earning $793,650 or more.
Federal income tax brackets show how much you owe on each part of your taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income.
The standard deduction will also increase in 2027, rising to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up from $32,200 in 2026. Starting in 2027, single filers can claim $16,600, a bump up from $16,100.
The new tax brackets come as Americans wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing , groceries , gasoline and other living expenses.
The consumer price index climbed 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from a yearly pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
The U.S. federal income tax system is progressive, which means tax rates increase as earnings rise.
For 2027, the federal brackets include seven income tiers, with rates ranging from 10% to 37%. The tax rates apply to each band of income rather than a flat percentage for all earnings.
The IRS adjusts the income ranges for each tax rate yearly based on the consumer price index.
Your federal tax brackets depend on your filing status , which you choose on your tax return. The options include single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse.
You can find your 2025 taxable income on line 15 of your individual federal income tax return, known as Form 1040 .

articles.title_zh: The Nasdaq Plunges 5%. What the Data Center Crash Means for Investors
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Is the AI bubble bursting?
That question was on the minds of millions of investors on Thursday, as the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) had one of its worst days ever, plunging 5.5% as fears spread that a political backlash could choke the AI boom, following the midterm election.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Investors believe that election winners in Texas and elsewhere will slap significant restrictions or even outright bans on data centers, which became a lightning rod during the campaign. After chip stocks were among the few losers on Wednesday, they collapsed on Thursday, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF losing 11.2%. Even industry leader Nvidia lost 9.1%, and the crash triggered a broader sell-off across the stock market, with all 11 sectors falling, even defensive ones like utilities and consumer staples.
Image source: Getty Images.
AI infrastructure stocks began to wobble a few weeks ago, starting with a chart showing that neocloud operator CoreWeave's (NASDAQ:CRWV) bond yields had risen as high as 15%, and worries about a potential default sent the stock tumbling.
Earnings reports from the big hyperscalers were greeted similarly, as investors worried about soaring capital expenditures and negative free cash flow, even as these companies continue to grow rapidly and are hugely profitable.
Then, the election happened, and now fears of a slowdown in the data center build-out have led investors to flee AI stocks .
Stock market reactions to elections are famously rash and often fleeting. Stocks tumbled following the Brexit decision before bouncing back over the following days, and stocks plunged overnight when President Trump was first elected before turning green the following day.
This looks like a similar reaction. Tech stocks initially fell on Tuesday night before the Nasdaq jumped on Wednesday. The response is understandable as data centers have been a major talking point during the campaign, but the sell-off seems like an overreaction.
Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, campaigned on a temporary moratorium on data centers and reasonable guidelines, like a ban on subsidies for data centers. However, she is no radical, telling CNN, "We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections."
In a worst-case scenario with a significant slowdown in data center construction in the U.S., most industry observers believe that activity would just move abroad, meaning that industry growth wouldn't be significantly impacted.
In an interview with the Motley Fool, Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) CFO Jason Child explained his thinking on the matter, saying, "Let's just say it (the data centers) all slows down. Do we believe AI demand will slow down? I think, generally, most people say no. The genie is out of the bottle." Child also said he was generally skeptical of any political reaction and said the bipartisan interest in economic growth was too strong for there to be a significant slowdown in the build-out. He also noted that Arm could still benefit from a slowdown in data center construction, as Arm's chips excel at performance per watt, which would be in greater demand if data center construction were artificially limited.
Predicting where the data center debate goes from here isn't easy, but Child is right that demand for AI is strong and is unlikely to be shaken by any slowdown in capacity growth.
Meanwhile, many of the top AI stocks are looking cheaper than ever. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) now trades at a forward P/E of less than 20, and it's nearly doubling its revenue each quarter. Micron (NASDAQ:MU), the memory chip leader, is trading at a forward P/E of less than 4.
Many of these AI stocks have already soared this year, so the pullback needs to be seen in that context, but like "Liberation Day" and other political issues that have rocked markets, this response seems likely to be an overreaction and a non-issue within the next year. Buying the dip on quality stocks like Nvidia looks like a smart move.

articles.content_orig:
The steep sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks likely has further to go, CNBC's Jim Cramer predicted Thursday — but he urged investors not to panic.
Growing opposition to new data centers following the midterm elections has raised doubts about future AI infrastructure spending, sending shares of companies tied to the buildout sharply lower. Micron tumbled 17%, GE Vernova dropped 7% and Sandisk plunged 22% on Thursday. All three stocks were also crushed in Wednesday's session.
"I wish I could say that today's flush was the bottom," the " Mad Money " host said, before cautioning that there may be more downside ahead, though he didn't believe this was an internet bubble redux. Cramer argued that today's AI companies are fundamentally different from the speculative businesses that collapsed during the dot-com bust.
"But I look at the charts, and there still seems like there's no support for so many Tech stocks, especially the semis, because they ran so much on the way up. However it might feel, it's actually an orderly decline because unlike 2000, these are mostly lucrative companies with stocks that went too high."
Investors had pushed AI stocks too high by assuming the rapid pace of data center construction would continue indefinitely, Cramer said. Smaller developers such as CoreWeave , Iren and Nebius face particular risks because they borrowed money to finance projects that could now face regulatory delays.
"That's what I am chiefly worried about," he said. "That's the real problem. That's what could really hurt the stock market. ... Right now, no one of significance is defaulting on their debt. The only issue with the debt is that it's connected to those neocloud companies that I mentioned. That's not enough to sink us."
Cramer suggested that a swift sell-off could help the market work off the excesses of the AI boom more effectively than a prolonged downturn.
"I for one am glad they are ripping the Band-Aid off this market rather than slowing trying to take it off a little bit each day," he said.
For investors, Cramer recommended maintaining sufficient cash. While semiconductor stocks could face further declines, he pointed to falling interest rates, signs of easing inflation and the possibility of an end to the Iran war as reasons for optimism.
"If you have cash you won't panic," Cramer concluded. "You won't be complacent, either. You will be clear-headed and that's how you will lose less money until things get better. They always do."
